This page is the interactive version of the lesson notes (PDF). Each section
starts with a problem in a game. Then it explains the idea behind it. It ends
with a **Do it** task and one set of questions. Every question on this page
has its answer: try first, then check.

## Key terms

{{< glossary vector-addition resultant-vector scalar-multiplication magnitude pythagorean-theorem unit-vector normalization speed velocity dot-product perpendicular angle-between-vectors forward-vector field-of-view >}}

## 2.1 Two moves at once: adding vectors

- A raft paddles across a river, and the river pushes it. The raft makes two
  moves in every frame.
- Draw the second arrow from the head of the first: **head to tail**.
- The arrow from the first tail to the last head is the **sum** (the
  **resultant**).
- Rule: add the x-parts, and add the y-parts:
  a + b = (a~x~ + b~x~, a~y~ + b~y~). The order does not matter.
- A game can add more than two moves in one frame: walk + wind + jump.
- Reverse question: the move you need = the move you want − the move you
  have.

![Paddle (0, 3) + current (2, 0) = real move (2, 3).](images/vector-add.png){width=72%}

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out!"}
(2, 0) + (0, 3) is **not** 5. The sum of two vectors is a vector: (2, 3).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Head to tail in GeoGebra"}
At geogebra.org/calculator, type `u = Vector((3, 1))`, `v = Vector((1, 2))`
and `w = Vector((3, 1), (4, 3))`. Then type `u + v`. Does it end where w
ends? Write the components of u + v.

::: {.check}
u + v = (3 + 1, 1 + 2) = (4, 3). Yes: w is v drawn from the head of u, and it
ends at (4, 3) too.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 1 · Adding moves"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="(2, 2)|5|(4, 3)"}
A raft paddles (0, 3). The current is (2, 0). The real move per frame?
:   (2, 3)

    Why: (0 + 2, 3 + 0) = (2, 3).

In one frame a character walks (3, 0), the wind pushes (−1, 0) and a jump lifts (0, 4). The total move?
:   (2, 4)

    Why: x: 3 − 1 + 0 = 2; y: 0 + 0 + 4 = 4.

What is (1, 0, 2) + (0, 4, −1)?
:   (1, 4, 1)

    Why: add each of the three parts: (1 + 0, 0 + 4, 2 − 1).

The current is (2, 0). Which paddle vector gives the move (0, 3)?
:   (−2, 3)

    Why: wanted − current = (0, 3) − (2, 0) = (−2, 3).

What is (−3, 2) + (3, −2)?
:   (0, 0)

    Why: a vector plus its opposite is the zero vector.
:::
:::

## 2.2 Faster, slower, backwards: scaling a vector

- To scale a vector by a number k, multiply **both** components by k:
  k v = (k v~x~, k v~y~).
- k > 1: a longer arrow (a dash power-up, × 2).
- 0 < k < 1: a shorter arrow (slow motion, × 0.5).
- k = −1: the same length, the opposite direction (a ball bounces back).
- After n frames, an object has moved n × v: the velocity scaled by n.

![v = (2, 1) scaled by 2, by 0.5 and by −1.](images/scaling.png){width=80%}

{{< sim file="sims/vector-lab.html" poster="sims/vector-lab.png" title="Vector Lab: scale, measure and normalize a vector" height="640" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Scale it in Vector Lab"}
In **Vector Lab**, drag the arrow to v = (2, 1). Set k to 3, then 0.5, then
−2. Write down k v each time. Which values of k reverse the arrow?

::: {.check}
3v = (6, 3), 0.5v = (1, 0.5), −2v = (−4, −2). Only a negative k reverses the
arrow.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 2 · Scaling"}
A character runs with v = (3, 1) per frame. Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="(6, 1)|(3, −1)|(−6, −2)"}
A dash power-up doubles the velocity. The new velocity?
:   (6, 2)

    Why: both parts × 2: (3 × 2, 1 × 2).

Slow motion halves the velocity. The new velocity?
:   (1.5, 0.5)

    Why: both parts × 0.5.

A wall throws the character straight back (× −1). The new velocity?
:   (−3, −1)

    Why: × −1 keeps the length and reverses the direction.

Which number k makes the arrow shorter, in the same direction?
:   k = 0.5

    Why: a k between 0 and 1 shortens the arrow without turning it.

The game is paused. It scales every velocity by…
:   0

    Why: 0 × v is the zero vector: nothing moves.
:::
:::

## 2.3 How far away is it? The magnitude

- A guard attacks when the player is at most 5 units away. The game needs
  the **length** of the vector from the guard to the player.
- The components and the arrow make a right-angled triangle.
- **Pythagorean theorem:** |v| = √(v~x~² + v~y~²).
- In 3D: |v| = √(v~x~² + v~y~² + v~z~²).
- (−3)² = 9, so (3, 4), (−3, 4) and (3, −4) all have the length 5.

![(3, 4) is 5 units long: 3² + 4² = 25 = 5².](images/magnitude.png){width=56%}

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out!"}
|(3, 4)| is **not** 3 + 4 = 7. The arrow goes straight across the triangle:
5.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Measure an arrow on paper"}
On squared paper (1 cm = 1 unit), draw the vector (6, 8). Measure it with a
ruler. Then calculate √(6² + 8²). Why is the arrow shorter than 6 + 8?

::: {.check}
√(36 + 64) = √100 = 10: the ruler shows about 10 cm. The arrow is the short
way straight across; 6 + 8 = 14 is the long way along the two sides.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 3 · How far?"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="7|25|−9"}
The magnitude of (3, −4).
:   5

    Why: √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5; the minus sign disappears when you square it.

The magnitude of (0, −9).
:   9

    Why: √(0 + 81) = 9. A length is never negative.

The magnitude of (−5, 12).
:   13

    Why: √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13.

Guard G = (1, 1), player P = (4, 5). The guard attacks at 5 units or less. Does it attack?
:   yes, the distance is 5

    Why: P − G = (3, 4), length 5, and 5 ≤ 5.

A drone flies (2, 3, 6). How far?
:   7

    Why: √(4 + 9 + 36) = √49 = 7.
:::
:::

## 2.4 Only the direction: unit vectors

- An arrow on the screen points to the goal. It always has the same size.
  The game needs only the **direction**.
- A **unit vector** has the length 1. It shows only a direction.
- **Normalize** = divide by the magnitude: v̂ = v ÷ |v|.
- Example: (6, 8) ÷ 10 = (0.6, 0.8).
- Easy ones: (1, 0) right, (0, 1) up, (0, −7) → (0, −1).
- The zero vector (0, 0) has no direction. It cannot be normalized.
- **Speed in a direction:** v = speed × d̂. A missile flies from (2, 1) to
  (8, 9) at speed 5: d̂ = (0.6, 0.8), so v = (3, 4). Normalize first, then the
  speed is the same in every direction.

![(6, 8) and its unit vector (0.6, 0.8) on the circle of radius 1.](images/unit-vector.png){width=64%}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Normalize in Vector Lab"}
In **Vector Lab**, switch on **Show unit vector**. Drag the arrow to (6, 8),
(0, −5) and (5, 12). Write the magnitude and the unit vector each time.

::: {.check}
(6, 8): 10 and (0.6, 0.8). (0, −5): 5 and (0, −1). (5, 12): 13 and about
(0.38, 0.92). Each unit vector has length 1: 0.6² + 0.8² = 1.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 4 · Unit vectors"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="(0, 7)|10|(1, 1)"}
Normalize (6, 8).
:   (0.6, 0.8)

    Why: the length is 10; (6 ÷ 10, 8 ÷ 10).

Normalize (0, −7).
:   (0, −1)

    Why: the length is 7; it points straight down, with length 1.

Scale the unit vector (0.6, 0.8) back to the length 10.
:   (6, 8)

    Why: 10 × (0.6, 0.8) = (6, 8).

What is the magnitude of every unit vector?
:   1

    Why: that is what "unit" means.

The player stands on the goal. Why can the game not normalize the vector to the goal?
:   it is the zero vector

    Why: its length is 0, and the game cannot divide by 0.
:::
:::

## 2.5 One number from two vectors: the dot product

- Does the wind help a boat, or slow it down? The game needs one number.
- The **dot product** multiplies the matching components and adds them:
  a · b = a~x~ b~x~ + a~y~ b~y~. In 3D, add a~z~ b~z~ too.
- The result is a **number** (a scalar), not a vector. The order does not
  matter.
- A boat moves (1, 0) and the wind is (3, 1): (1, 0) · (3, 1) = 3. Positive,
  so the wind helps the boat.

![(1, 0) · (3, 1) = 1 × 3 + 0 × 1 = 3.](images/dot-steps.png){width=80%}

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out!"}
The products (3 and 0) are only a middle step. The dot product is their sum:
**3**, not (3, 0).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · The dot product in GeoGebra"}
At geogebra.org/calculator, type `u = Vector((2, 3))`, `v = Vector((4, -1))`
and then `u * v`. Calculate (2, 3) · (4, −1) by hand. Do the two numbers
agree?

::: {.check}
2 × 4 + 3 × (−1) = 8 − 3 = 5. GeoGebra shows 5 too.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 5 · Compute it"}
Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="(3, 0)|(8, −3)|−1"}
The boat moves (1, 0). The wind is (3, 1). The dot product?
:   3

    Why: 1 × 3 + 0 × 1 = 3.

(2, 3) · (4, −1)
:   5

    Why: 8 + (−3) = 5.

(1, 2, 3) · (4, 0, −1)
:   1

    Why: 4 + 0 − 3 = 1: in 3D, add three products.

(−2, 5) · (3, 1)
:   −1

    Why: −6 + 5 = −1.

What kind of result does a dot product give?
:   one number

    Why: the products are added into one scalar.
:::
:::

## 2.6 In front or behind? The sign of the dot product

- A guard's **forward vector** f shows where it looks.
- The vector from the guard to the cat: d = C − D.
- f · d **positive**: the angle is less than 90°. The cat is in front.
- f · d **zero**: exactly 90°. The cat is exactly to the side: d is
  **perpendicular** to f.
- f · d **negative**: more than 90°. The cat is behind.
- The same test with the velocity: positive = moving towards the goal.

![The sign of f · d: in front, to the side, behind.](images/dot-sign.png){width=84%}

{{< sim file="sims/dot-lab.html" poster="sims/dot-lab.png" title="Dot Lab: two vectors, one number" height="640" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Dot Lab"}
In **Dot Lab**, drag the orange arrow until the dot product is positive,
then zero, then negative. Write the two vectors and the dot product each
time. Where is the orange arrow when the result is zero?

::: {.check}
Positive: in front (less than 90°). Zero: exactly at a right angle, to the
side. Negative: behind (more than 90°).
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 6 · In front or behind?"}
A guard dog at D = (2, 2) faces f = (1, 0). Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="far away|above the dog"}
A cat at (5, 3). Where is it?
:   in front

    Why: d = (3, 1), f · d = 3: positive.

A cat at (0, 4). Where is it?
:   behind

    Why: d = (−2, 2), f · d = −2: negative.

A cat at (2, 6). Where is it?
:   exactly to the side

    Why: d = (0, 4), f · d = 0: a right angle.

The dot product of two vectors is negative. The angle between them is…
:   more than 90°

    Why: a negative sign means the arrows point more away than together.

A player at (1, 1) moves (−1, 2). The treasure is at (4, 5). Is the player moving towards it?
:   yes, the dot product is 5

    Why: to the treasure (3, 4); (−1, 2) · (3, 4) = −3 + 8 = 5.

Are (4, 6) and (−3, 2) perpendicular?
:   yes, the dot product is 0

    Why: −12 + 12 = 0 means a right angle.
:::
:::

## 2.7 How big is the angle?

- The dot product grows with the lengths. So first **normalize** both
  vectors.
- For two unit vectors, â · b̂ is a number from −1 to 1. It depends only on
  the angle.
- For any vectors: a · b ÷ (|a| × |b|).
- This number is the **cosine** of the angle (Lecture 4). For now, use the
  table:

| â · b̂ | 1 | 0.87 | 0.71 | 0.5 | 0 | −0.5 | −0.71 | −1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| angle | 0° | 30° | 45° | 60° | 90° | 120° | 135° | 180° |

![b̂ at four angles to â, with the value of â · b̂.](images/dot-angles.png){width=82%}

::: {.callout-warning title="Watch out!"}
(3, 0) · (2, 0) = 6, but the angle is 0°. Divide first: 6 ÷ (3 × 2) = 1, so
0°.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Find the angle in Dot Lab"}
In **Dot Lab**, switch on **Unit vectors**. Make the angle 0°, 60°, 90° and
180°. Write â · b̂ each time and compare with the table.

::: {.check}
0° → 1; 60° → 0.5; 90° → 0; 180° → −1, as in the table.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 7 · The angle"}
Use the table above. Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="6°|0.5°|30°"}
Two unit vectors have the dot product 0.5. The angle?
:   60°

    Why: the table gives 0.5 → 60°.

Two unit vectors have the dot product −1. The angle?
:   180°

    Why: −1 means exactly opposite directions.

The angle between (2, 0) and (0, 7).
:   90°

    Why: the dot product is 0 + 0 = 0, so a right angle.

A guard faces (1, 0). The cat is in the direction (3, 4), so â · b̂ = 0.6. The angle?
:   between 45° and 60°

    Why: 0.6 is between 0.5 (60°) and 0.71 (45°).

(3, 0) · (2, 0) = 6. What is the angle?
:   0°

    Why: 6 ÷ (3 × 2) = 1, and 1 means 0°.
:::
:::

## Game challenge: Shadow Cat {.challenge}

Work alone. Use every section of today.

**Shadow Cat** is a stealth game. A guard dog is at D = (6, 4) and looks
right: f = (1, 0). It sees a point at most 60° to the side (f̂ · d̂ ≥ 0.5)
and at most 5 units away. Bush A is at (10, 7), bush B at (9, 8) and bush C
at (6, 9). The fish is at (2, 1). The cat can hide only where the dog cannot
see it. Later the dog turns and looks up: f = (0, 1).

{{< sim file="sims/shadow-cat.html" poster="sims/shadow-cat.png" title="Shadow Cat: find the bush the dog cannot see" kind="game" height="680" >}}

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 8 · The dog looks right"}
Shadow Cat: dog D = (6, 4), f = (1, 0), 60° to each side, 5 units deep.
Bushes A (10, 7), B (9, 8), C (6, 9). Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="(3, 4)|A|0.6"}
The vector from the dog to bush A.
:   (4, 3)

    Why: A − D = (10 − 6, 7 − 4).

f · d for bush B, with d = (3, 4).
:   3

    Why: 1 × 3 + 0 × 4 = 3.

Which bush is safe for the cat?
:   C

    Why: C has d = (0, 5): f̂ · d̂ = 0, less than 0.5. A (0.8) and B (0.6) are seen.

The cat goes for the fish at (2, 1). Is it in front of the dog?
:   no, behind

    Why: d = (−4, −3), f · d = −4: negative.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it 9 · The dog turns (harder)"}
Shadow Cat: dog D = (6, 4), now f = (0, 1). Bushes A (10, 7), B (9, 8),
C (6, 9). Fish (2, 1). Choose the right answer.

::: {.match extra="(0, −1)|−0.8|0"}
The value f̂ · d̂ for bush C, with d̂ = (0, 1).
:   1

    Why: (0, 1) · (0, 1) = 1: C is straight ahead now.

The value f̂ · d̂ for bush A, with d̂ = (0.8, 0.6).
:   0.6

    Why: 0 × 0.8 + 1 × 0.6 = 0.6.

Is any bush safe now?
:   no, all three are seen

    Why: A 0.6, B 0.8, C 1: all ≥ 0.5, all 5 units away.

The value f̂ · d̂ for the fish, with d̂ = (−0.8, −0.6).
:   −0.6

    Why: 0 × (−0.8) + 1 × (−0.6) = −0.6: behind the dog.

Which vector is perpendicular to the new f = (0, 1)?
:   (−1, 0)

    Why: (0, 1) · (−1, 0) = 0.
:::
:::

## Summary {.summary}

- Add vectors part by part: (2, 0) + (0, 3) = (2, 3). Scale both parts: 2 × (3, 1) = (6, 2).
- The magnitude is the length: |(3, 4)| = √(9 + 16) = 5.
- A unit vector has length 1: v ÷ |v|. Velocity = speed × direction.
- The dot product a · b = a~x~ b~x~ + a~y~ b~y~ is one number.
- Positive: in front. Zero: perpendicular. Negative: behind.
- For unit vectors, â · b̂ gives the angle: 0.5 → 60°, 0 → 90°.
